heroHeadline: Hague Court Rules Indus Waters Treaty Still in Force; India Rejects Ruling as Shopian Hideout Busted
heroSubtitle: August 31, 2026: The Permanent Court of Arbitration at The Hague issued its merits award in the Pakistan-initiated Indus Waters Treaty case, ruling the 1960 treaty 'remains fully in force' and that none of India's stated grounds justified its April 2025 suspension; the Court found India's Kishenganga design changes breached the treaty and barred further concreting of the Ratle dam wall and intake structure until 90 days after a neutral expert's final decision, expected around July 2027. India's Ministry of External Affairs categorically rejected the award — 'This so-called Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India's sovereign decisions' — and reaffirmed the treaty stays in abeyance until Pakistan credibly ends cross-border terrorism support; Pakistan's Foreign Office welcomed the ruling and said it would give it 'careful consideration.' Separately on August 31, security forces busted a suspected militant hideout in Shopian's Naikpora Memender, recovering an AK-47, a pistol, a grenade and ammunition, with no arrests yet reported. On August 29-30, 25 Pakistani nationals including fishermen were released from Indian jails and repatriated via the Wagah-Attari border under the July 1 prisoner-list exchange. The LoC itself has seen no new firing or infiltration incidents since the August 27-29 drone cluster in Rajouri and Poonch; the ceasefire holds at Day 478 with no confirmed cross-border fire exchange since May 10, 2025. Bilateral freeze remains otherwise comprehensive: no ambassadors, $0 formal trade.
footerNote: Data sourced from Indian MEA/MOD, Pakistan ISPR/MFA, UN Security Council, SIPRI, Crisis Group, HRW, Stimson Center
